title: Surface Area of Combinations of Solids: The Hidden Interface Principle
description: Master the fundamental principle of combined surface areas: when two solids are joined together, their touching interface surfaces disappear inside and CANNOT be painted or touched. Therefore, Total Surface Area is the sum of the EXPOSED curved surface areas, NOT the sum of their individual total surface areas.
key_concepts: The Hidden Interface Principle: TSA of combined solid ≠ TSA of Solid 1 + TSA of Solid 2! Touching base faces are hidden inside and must NOT be included
Cone Mounted on Hemisphere (Toy): TSA = CSA of Cone + CSA of Hemisphere = πrl + 2πr²
Slant Height of Cone: l = √(r² + h²)
Cylinder with Two Hemispheres (Capsule): TSA = CSA of Cylinder + 2 × (CSA of Hemisphere) = 2πrh + 4πr² = 2πr(h + 2r)
Cubical Block Surmounted by Hemisphere: TSA = TSA of Cube - Area of Circular Base + CSA of Hemisphere = 6a² - πr² + 2πr² = 6a² + πr²
Hemispherical Depression Scooped Out: TSA = 6a² - πr² + 2πr² = 6a² + πr² (Identical surface area whether surmounted or scooped out!)
subtopics: Deconstructing composite 3D objects into elementary curved components
Calculating cone slant height l = √(r² + h²)
Worked Example 1, Example 2, Example 3 from NCERT

worked_examples.problem: Example 2 (NCERT): The decorative block shown in Fig. is made of two solids — a cube and a hemisphere. The base of the block is a cube with edge 5 cm, and the hemisphere fixed on the top has a diameter of 4.2 cm. Find the total surface area of the block. (Take π = 22/7)
worked_examples.solution:
Given:
Edge of the cubical block a = 5 cm.
Diameter of hemisphere d = 4.2 cm ⇒ Radius r = 4.2 / 2 = 2.1 cm.

Step 1: Understand the exposed surface area:
The block consists of 6 faces of the cube, EXCEPT the circular base of the hemisphere which covers part of the top face.
On top of that covered part sits the curved dome of the hemisphere.
Therefore:
Total Surface Area = (Total Surface Area of Cube) - (Base Area of Hemisphere) + (Curved Surface Area of Hemisphere)
= 6a² - πr² + 2πr²
= 6a² + πr².

Step 2: Calculate TSA of Cube:
6a² = 6 × (5)² = 6 × 25 = 150 cm².

Step 3: Calculate Net Additional Curved Area (πr²):
πr² = (22 / 7) × (2.1)²
= (22 / 7) × 4.41
= 22 × 0.63 = 13.86 cm².

Step 4: Compute Total Surface Area of the Decorative Block:
Total Surface Area = 150 + 13.86 = 163.86 cm².
[ROUGH_WORK]
6 × 25 = 150
22 × 0.63: 20 × 0.63 = 12.6, 2 × 0.63 = 1.26 ⇒ 12.6 + 1.26 = 13.86.
150 + 13.86 = 163.86 cm².
Boxed Answer: [ Total surface area of the block = 163.86 cm² ].
concept_questions: Why do we subtract πr² from 6a²?
What would be the surface area if a hemispherical cavity of the same diameter had been carved into the block?

title: Volume of Combinations of Solids: Additive Conservation & Liquid Displacement
description: Understand the additive conservation principle of volume: unlike surface area, volume is strictly additive and subtractive. Total volume of a composite solid is simply the algebraic sum of the individual component volumes (or total volume minus carved volume for cavities). Master liquid displacement in vessels.
key_concepts: Volume Additive Invariant: Volume is always conserved; Total Volume = Volume(Solid 1) + Volume(Solid 2)
Cavity Volume: When a cavity is scooped out, Remaining Volume = Original Solid Volume - Cavity Volume
Cylinder Volume: V = πr²h
Cone Volume: V = 1/3 πr²h
Sphere Volume: V = 4/3 πr³
Hemisphere Volume: V = 2/3 πr³
Archimedes Liquid Displacement: Volume of water overflowing = Total volume of submerged solids
subtopics: Additive volume property for combined solids
Subtractive volume property for hollowed cavities

worked_examples.problem: Example 6 (NCERT): A juice seller was serving his customers using glasses as shown in Fig. The inner diameter of the cylindrical glass was 5 cm, but the bottom of the glass had a hemispherical raised portion which reduced the capacity of the glass. If the height of a glass was 10 cm, find the apparent capacity of the glass and its actual capacity. (Use π = 3.14)
worked_examples.solution:
Given:
Inner diameter of cylindrical glass d = 5 cm ⇒ Radius r = 5 / 2 = 2.5 cm.
Height of glass h = 10 cm.
Value of π = 3.14.

Step 1: Calculate Apparent Capacity (Apparent Volume = Volume of Cylinder):
Apparent Capacity = πr²h
= 3.14 × (2.5)² × 10
= 3.14 × 6.25 × 10
= 3.14 × 62.5 = 196.25 cm³.

Step 2: Calculate Volume of Hemispherical Raised Bottom:
Volume of Hemisphere = 2/3 πr³
= (2 / 3) × 3.14 × (2.5)³
= (2 / 3) × 3.14 × 15.625
= (2 / 3) × 49.0625
= 98.125 / 3 ≈ 32.71 cm³.

Step 3: Calculate Actual Capacity (Net Available Volume):
Actual Capacity = (Apparent Capacity) - (Volume of Hemispherical Dome)
= 196.25 - 32.71 = 163.54 cm³.
[ROUGH_WORK]
Apparent = 196.25 cm³, Actual = 163.54 cm³.
The customer receives 32.71 cm³ less juice than appears!
Boxed Answer: [ Apparent capacity = 196.25 cm³, Actual capacity = 163.54 cm³ ].

description: Complete step-by-step resolution of NCERT Exercise 12.1 Questions 1 through 9. Ex 12.1 Q2: Vessel: Hemisphere d = 14 cm (r = 7 cm), Total H = 13 cm ⇒ Cylinder h = 13 - 7 = 6 cm ⇒ Inner SA = 2πrh + 2πr² = 2πr(h + r) = 2 × (22/7) × 7 × 13 = 572 cm²

Ex 12.1 Q4: Block side 7 cm: Greatest hemisphere d = 7 cm (r = 3.5 cm) ⇒ TSA = 6(49) + π(3.5)² = 294 + 38.5 = 332.5 cm²
Ex 12.1 Q5: Hemispherical depression edge l: TSA = 6l² + π(l/2)² = (l²/4)(24 + π)

worked_examples.problem: Exercise 12.1 Q6: A medicine capsule is in the shape of a cylinder with two hemispheres stuck to each of its ends. The length of the entire capsule is 14 mm and the diameter of the capsule is 5 mm. Find its surface area.
worked_examples.solution:
Given:
Diameter of capsule d = 5 mm ⇒ Radius r = 5 / 2 = 2.5 mm.
Total length of entire capsule = 14 mm.

Step 1: Find height (length) of the cylindrical portion 'h':
The two hemispherical ends each contribute their radius r to the total length:
Total length = r + h + r = h + 2r
14 = h + 2(2.5) = h + 5
h = 14 - 5 = 9 mm.

Step 2: Formulate Total Surface Area of the Capsule:
The total surface area is the sum of the curved surface area of the cylinder and the two hemispherical ends:
TSA = CSA of Cylinder + 2 × (CSA of Hemisphere)
= 2πrh + 2 × (2πr²)
= 2πrh + 4πr²
= 2πr (h + 2r).

Step 3: Substitute known values (notice h + 2r = 14 mm, the total length!):
TSA = 2 × (22 / 7) × (2.5) × (9 + 5)
= 2 × (22 / 7) × 2.5 × 14
Cancel 14 with 7 in denominator (14 / 7 = 2):
= 2 × 22 × 2.5 × 2
= 44 × 5 = 220 mm².
[ROUGH_WORK]
2 × 2.5 = 5; 44 × 5 = 220 mm².
Clean, elegant, zero rounding errors!
Boxed Answer: [ Surface area of capsule = 220 mm² ].
concept_questions: Why does the cylinder length equal 14 - 5 = 9 mm?
Why are the two circular bases of the cylinder not included in the surface area?

worked_examples.problem: Exercise 12.2 Q3: A gulab jamun, contains sugar syrup up to about 30% of its volume. Find approximately how much syrup would be found in 45 gulab jamuns, each shaped like a cylinder with two hemispherical ends with length 5 cm and diameter 2.8 cm.
worked_examples.solution:
Given:
Diameter of gulab jamun d = 2.8 cm ⇒ Radius r = 2.8 / 2 = 1.4 cm.
Total length of gulab jamun = 5 cm.
Percentage of syrup = 30% of total volume.
Number of gulab jamuns = 45.

Step 1: Find height (length) of the cylindrical portion 'h':
h = Total length - 2r = 5 - 2(1.4) = 5 - 2.8 = 2.2 cm.

Step 2: Calculate Volume of ONE Gulab Jamun:
Volume = Volume of Cylinder + 2 × (Volume of Hemisphere)
= πr²h + 2 × (2/3 πr³)
= πr² [ h + 4/3 r ].
Substitute r = 1.4 = 7/5, h = 2.2 = 11/5, π = 22/7:
Volume = (22 / 7) × (1.4)² × [ 2.2 + (4 / 3) × 1.4 ]
= (22 / 7) × 1.96 × [ 2.2 + 1.867 ]
= 22 × 0.28 × [ 4.067 ]
= 6.16 × 4.067 ≈ 25.05 cm³.

Step 3: Calculate Volume of 45 Gulab Jamuns:
Total Volume = 45 × 25.05 = 1127.28 cm³.

Step 4: Calculate Volume of Sugar Syrup (30% of Total Volume):
Syrup Volume = 30% of 1127.28
= (30 / 100) × 1127.28
= 0.30 × 1127.28 = 338.184 cm³ ≈ 338 cm³.
[ROUGH_WORK]
45 × 6.16 × (6.6 + 5.6)/3 = 15 × 6.16 × 12.2 = 1127.28.
0.30 × 1127.28 = 338.18 ≈ 338 cm³.
Boxed Answer: [ Volume of sugar syrup in 45 gulab jamuns ≈ 338 cm³ ].

worked_examples.problem: Exercise 12.2 Q5: A vessel is in the form of an inverted cone. Its height is 8 cm and the radius of its top, which is open, is 5 cm. It is filled with water up to the brim. When lead shots, each of which is a sphere of radius 0.5 cm are dropped into the vessel, one-fourth of the water flows out. Find the number of lead shots dropped into the vessel.
worked_examples.solution:
Given:
Inverted cone: Radius R = 5 cm, Height H = 8 cm.
Vessel is full of water up to brim.
Lead shots: Spheres of radius r = 0.5 cm.
Fraction of water displaced = 1/4 of total volume of cone.

Step 1: Calculate Volume of Water in the Cone:
Volume of Cone = 1/3 π R² H
= (1 / 3) × π × (5)² × 8
= (1 / 3) × π × 25 × 8
= 200π / 3 cm³.

Step 2: Calculate Volume of Water that Flows Out:
Volume displaced = 1/4 × Volume of Cone
= (1 / 4) × (200π / 3) = 50π / 3 cm³.

Step 3: Calculate Volume of ONE Spherical Lead Shot:
Volume of 1 lead shot = 4/3 π r³
= (4 / 3) × π × (0.5)³
= (4 / 3) × π × 0.125
= (4 / 3) × π × (1 / 8)
= π / 6 cm³.

Step 4: Find Number of Lead Shots 'n' using Archimedes Principle:
By Archimedes Principle:
Total volume of 'n' lead shots = Volume of water displaced
n × (Volume of 1 lead shot) = Volume of water that flowed out
n × (π / 6) = 50π / 3
Divide both sides by π:
n / 6 = 50 / 3
n = (50 × 6) / 3 = 50 × 2 = 100 lead shots!
[ROUGH_WORK]
Notice π cancels out entirely! Never approximate π = 3.14 or 22/7 until the very end.
n = (50/3) / (1/6) = (50/3) × 6 = 100.
Boxed Answer: [ Number of lead shots dropped = 100 ].

What fraction of water would flow out if 200 lead shots were dropped?

title: Industrial Modeling, Structural Optimization & Mass-Density Formulations
description: Master real-world industrial and physical applications of surface areas and volumes: computing iron pole mass using density (Mass = Volume × Density), structural canvas requirements, packaging optimization, and verifying complex container capacities with rigorous dimensional checks.
key_concepts: Density to Mass Conversion: Mass = Volume × Density (e.g. 1 cm³ of iron = 8 g ⇒ Mass in kg = Volume × 8 / 1000)
Structural Compound Models: Rachel's engineering rocket model (Cylinder with conical nose and tail)
Dimensional Consistency Check: Volume is cubic units (cm³, m³), Surface area is square units (cm², m²); 1 m³ = 1,000,000 cm³ = 1000 Litres
Ratio of Shapes: Sphere inscribed in a cylinder has Volume(Sphere) : Volume(Cylinder) = 2 : 3 and SA(Sphere) : TSA(Cylinder) = 2 : 3 (Archimedes' tombstone theorem!)

worked_examples.problem: Exercise 12.2 Q6: A solid iron pole consists of a cylinder of height 220 cm and base diameter 24 cm, which is surmounted by another cylinder of height 60 cm and radius 8 cm. Find the mass of the pole, given that 1 cm³ of iron has approximately 8 g mass. (Use π = 3.14)
worked_examples.solution:
Given:
Lower cylinder: Height H = 220 cm, Diameter D = 24 cm ⇒ Radius R = 12 cm.
Upper cylinder: Height h = 60 cm, Radius r = 8 cm.
Density of iron = 8 g per cm³.
Value of π = 3.14.

Step 1: Calculate Volume of Lower Cylinder:
V1 = π R² H
= 3.14 × (12)² × 220
= 3.14 × 144 × 220
= 3.14 × 31680 = 99475.2 cm³.

Step 2: Calculate Volume of Upper Cylinder:
V2 = π r² h
= 3.14 × (8)² × 60
= 3.14 × 64 × 60
= 3.14 × 3840 = 12057.6 cm³.

Step 3: Calculate Total Volume of the Iron Pole:
Total Volume V = V1 + V2
= 99475.2 + 12057.6 = 111532.8 cm³.

Step 4: Calculate Mass of the Pole:
Mass = Volume × Density
= 111532.8 × 8 grams
= 892262.4 grams.

Step 5: Convert Mass into Kilograms (1 kg = 1000 g):
Mass = 892262.4 / 1000
= 892.2624 kg ≈ 892.26 kg.
[ROUGH_WORK]
Alternative factoring: π [ (144 × 220) + (64 × 60) ] = 3.14 × [ 31680 + 3840 ] = 3.14 × 35520 = 111532.8 cm³.
111532.8 × 8 = 892262.4 g = 892.26 kg.
Boxed Answer: [ Mass of iron pole ≈ 892.26 kg ].

How many cubic centimeters are in one cubic meter?
